Large images are the single most common reason a web page loads slowly, an e-mail bounces or an online form refuses your upload. Unlike most online compressors, nothing is uploaded. The work happens inside your browser, so it is as fast as your device, has no daily limit and is safe for passport scans, medical photos, contracts photographed on a phone and anything else you would rather not hand to a stranger's server.
What you can do here that most compressors don't offer

**Compress to an exact file size.** Government portals, job sites, exam registration forms and visa applications often say 'photo under 50 KB' or 'signature under 20 KB'. Choose the target and the tool finds the best quality that fits; if quality alone cannot get there, it gently reduces the pixel dimensions until it does.

**Resize in the same step.** Set a maximum width (for example 1920 px for a website hero image or 1080 px for social media) and the image is scaled down before compression – the biggest saving of all for phone photos.
**Strip metadata.** EXIF data such as GPS location, camera serial number and editing history is removed by default. That protects your privacy and shaves extra kilobytes.
**Batch with a report.** Compress many images at once and get a table with the original size, new size and percentage saved for each file, plus one ZIP download.
**Never bigger than the original.** If an image is already optimised and cannot be made smaller in the same format, you get the original back instead of a larger file.
**Works offline and has no caps.** No 5 MB per-file limit, no 20-image limit, no account and no watermark.
How to compress an image
Drop your JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, HEIC, GIF or BMP files onto the page, or press Ctrl+V to paste a screenshot from the clipboard.
Choose a quality level, or pick a target file size such as 50 KB or 100 KB.
Optionally choose an output format (keep original, JPG, WebP, PNG or AVIF) and a maximum width.
Click Compress. Single images download directly; several images come back in one ZIP with a size report.
How image compression works
Digital photos contain far more information than the human eye can detect at normal viewing size. Compression exploits this in two ways.

**Lossy compression** (JPG, WebP, AVIF) discards fine detail that you are unlikely to notice: subtle colour variation inside smooth areas like skies and skin, and high-frequency texture that is lost anyway when an image is viewed on a phone screen. JPG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks, converts each block into frequencies and rounds off the less important ones; the quality setting controls how aggressive that rounding is. WebP and AVIF use more modern prediction techniques borrowed from video codecs, so they reach the same visual quality with considerably fewer bytes.

**Lossless compression** (PNG) keeps every pixel exactly. The file gets smaller only by describing the same pixels more efficiently. To make PNGs dramatically smaller, {brand} uses colour quantisation: it reduces the image to an optimised palette of up to 256 colours, chosen to represent the original as closely as possible, and then stores it losslessly. For logos, icons, charts, screenshots and illustrations this typically cuts the size by 60–80% with no visible change, and transparency is preserved.

Resizing has the largest effect of all. Halving the width and height of an image removes three quarters of its pixels, so a 4000-pixel phone photo scaled to 1600 pixels is already around 85% smaller before any compression is applied.

Compressing images to a specific KB size

Many official forms specify a maximum file size for photos and signatures. Indian exam and recruitment portals, passport and visa systems, university applications and bank KYC forms commonly ask for something like 'photo 20–50 KB, signature 10–20 KB, JPG only'. Hitting those numbers by trial and error in a photo editor is tedious.

Choose the target from the list (or 'Custom' and type the number) and the compressor runs a binary search on the quality setting: it encodes the image, checks the size, and narrows down until it finds the highest quality that is still under your limit. If even low quality is too large – a big 12-megapixel photo cannot fit into 20 KB at full size – it reduces the pixel dimensions step by step until it fits. PNG images are saved as WebP or JPG in this mode because lossless PNG cannot be squeezed to a fixed size.

If the form also specifies exact pixel dimensions (for example 200×230 px), first use [Resize Image](/resize-image/) with the right preset or size, then compress the result to the KB target – or use the 'Max file size' box in the resize tool to do both at once.
Why compress images for your website?

Images usually make up the largest share of a page's weight. Smaller images mean faster loading, which improves user experience, conversions and search visibility – Google uses page experience signals such as Largest Contentful Paint, and the largest element on most pages is an image. Lighter pages also cost less to serve and are kinder to visitors on slow mobile data.
Serve images no wider than the largest size they are displayed at – a 1200 px wide content column never needs a 4000 px image.
Prefer WebP or AVIF for photos; keep PNG or SVG for logos and icons.
Use quality 65–75 for most web photos; the difference from 90 is rarely visible on screen.
Strip metadata – browsers do not need camera details, and GPS data can reveal where a photo was taken.
Lazy-load images below the fold so they only download when the visitor scrolls.
Compressing a gallery of product photos from 3 MB each to around 150 KB each can turn a page that takes ten seconds on a phone into one that appears almost instantly.
Will compression reduce quality?

At sensible settings, not visibly. Quality 75–85 JPG or WebP is indistinguishable from the original for most people when viewed at normal size. Artefacts become noticeable at very low quality – blockiness in smooth gradients, halos around sharp edges and smeared fine texture. If you see them, raise the quality or allow a slightly larger target size.

Re-compressing an already compressed JPG again and again does slowly degrade it, because each pass discards a little more detail. Always start from the best original you have, and keep that original safe. Screenshots and graphics with sharp text compress best as PNG palette images or high-quality WebP; JPG tends to blur text edges.
Metadata, orientation and colour

Photos from phones store their orientation in EXIF data rather than rotating the pixels. The compressor applies that orientation before saving, so the result is the right way up even after the metadata is removed. GPS coordinates, camera model, lens details and timestamps are discarded when 'Remove metadata' is on, which is the default; untick it if you need to keep them.

Images are converted to the standard sRGB colour space used by the web. Transparent areas are preserved in PNG, WebP and AVIF output; when saving to JPG, which cannot store transparency, transparent areas are filled with white.
Supported formats and limits

Input: JPG/JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, GIF (first frame), BMP, TIFF, ICO, SVG and HEIC/HEIF photos from iPhones. Output: JPG, PNG, WebP or AVIF. There is no fixed file-size or file-count limit; the practical limit is your device's memory. A typical laptop handles batches of hundreds of photos and individual images up to about 100 megapixels. Very large batches are processed one image at a time, so your browser stays responsive.
Privacy: your images never leave your device

Every step happens inside your browser tab. The image is decoded, edited and re-encoded on your own device using the browser's built-in image engine and WebAssembly, and the result is handed straight to your downloads folder. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is stored on a server and there is no queue, so private photos, ID cards, screenshots with personal data and unreleased product shots never leave your computer or phone. You can even switch off Wi‑Fi once the page has loaded and the tool keeps working.

Many popular online compressors upload your files to their servers and keep them for a period before deletion – TinyPNG, for example, states that it retains uploads for up to 48 hours. With {brand} there is simply nothing to retain.
Compressing images for online shops and marketplaces

Marketplaces such as Amazon, Etsy, eBay, Flipkart and Shopify stores all recommend large, sharp product photos – often 1600–2500 pixels on the long side so customers can zoom – but they also reward fast pages. The best approach is to export each product photo once at the recommended dimensions, then compress at quality 80–85. The zoomed view stays crisp, and the file usually drops from several megabytes to 200–400 KB. For your own store, also create WebP copies at 800–1200 px for category pages and thumbnails, where nobody zooms and every kilobyte counts.

Keep backgrounds clean and evenly lit: plain white or light grey backgrounds compress far better than textured tables or fabric, and they look more professional. If you need a pure white background, [Remove Background](/remove-background/) can replace it before you compress.
Screen versus print

Compression settings for screens and for print are different. Screens show roughly 100–200 pixels per inch at normal viewing distance, so web images can be modest in size and use moderate quality. Printers need around 300 pixels per inch at the final print size: an A4 photo print needs roughly 2480×3508 pixels. For print, keep the full resolution, use quality 90 or higher and stay with JPG, which every print shop accepts. Never print from an image that was compressed to a small KB target for a web form – the lost detail cannot be recovered.
If you only have a small image and need a larger print, [Upscale Image](/upscale-image/) can enlarge it with sharpening, which is better than letting the printer stretch it.
Compressing GIFs and animations

This tool saves the first frame of an animated GIF as a still image. To keep the animation, use [Compress GIF](/compress-gif/), which reduces colours and frame size while preserving motion, or convert short clips to MP4 or WebP video for files that are often ten times smaller than the GIF.
Compressing on phones and tablets

The compressor works in Safari on iPhone and iPad and in Chrome on Android. Tap the drop area to pick photos from your gallery – iPhone HEIC photos are converted automatically – and the compressed images are saved to your downloads or Files app. Because processing happens on the phone, large batches may take a little longer on older devices, but nothing uses your mobile data for uploads.

Tips for the smallest possible files
Crop first. Removing empty borders reduces both pixels and bytes.
Resize before compressing – it is the biggest single saving.
Choose WebP or AVIF if the destination accepts it.

Removing a background used to mean twenty minutes with the pen tool in Photoshop. {brand}'s background remover does it in seconds: drop a photo and an AI model finds the main subject – a person, a product, a pet, a car – and separates it from everything behind it. Download the cut-out as a transparent PNG, or put it straight onto a clean white background, a brand colour, a blurred version of the original, or a completely different photo of your choice.

The difference from the well-known services is where the work happens. The segmentation model runs inside your browser using WebAssembly, so your photo is never uploaded. That makes it suitable for ID photos, pictures of children, confidential product prototypes and anything else you would not post to a public server – and it means there are no credits, no paid 'HD download' and no account.
Features
**Transparent PNG** at up to 4096 pixels on the long side – no low-resolution preview limit.
**Replace the background** with white (for marketplaces), any solid colour, a soft blur of the original scene, or your own background image.
**Soft or sharp edges** – soft edges look natural on hair and fur; sharp edges are cleaner for products with hard outlines.

How to remove the background from an image
Drop one or more photos (JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC and more) or paste one with Ctrl+V.
Choose what should replace the background: transparent, white, a colour, blurred original or your own image.
Choose soft or sharp edges.
Click Remove background. The first run loads the AI model; later images are faster.
Download the PNG (transparent) or JPG (with a new background), or the ZIP for a batch.
How the AI background remover works

The tool uses U²-Net, a neural network designed for 'salient object detection' – finding the thing in a photo that a person would naturally look at. The image is scaled to 320×320 pixels and passed through the network, which outputs a probability for every pixel of being foreground. That low-resolution mask is then scaled back up to the full size of your photo with smooth interpolation, so the final cut-out keeps the full detail of the original image, not the size the network saw.

With soft edges, the mask is lightly feathered so semi-transparent pixels at the boundary blend smoothly into any new background – important for hair, fur and motion blur. With sharp edges, every pixel is either fully kept or fully removed, which gives crisp outlines for boxes, bottles and electronics.
Because the model runs on your device, speed depends on your hardware: a modern laptop processes a photo in one to three seconds, a phone in a few seconds more.
Best uses
**E-commerce product photos** – white backgrounds for Amazon, Flipkart, eBay and Etsy listings, or consistent brand-colour backgrounds for your own shop.
**Profile pictures** – a clean, professional look for LinkedIn, CVs and company websites.
**ID and visa photos** – replace a cluttered room with a plain white or light blue background, then size it with [Passport Photo Maker](/passport-photo-maker/).
**Design and marketing** – cut-outs for posters, thumbnails, presentations and social media graphics.

**Real estate and cars** – isolate a car or a piece of furniture for a listing.

Use a photo where the subject is clearly separated from the background – some distance and contrast helps.
Good, even lighting avoids shadows being treated as part of the subject.
Keep the whole subject in frame; cut-off edges are fine but the model works best when the main object is obvious.
For group photos, the model keeps everything it considers the main subject; crop first if you want just one person.
For fine hair against a busy background, choose soft edges and a background colour close to the original for the most natural result.
If a small area is wrong, open the PNG in an editor and touch it up – the hard work is already done.
Transparent PNG or JPG?

A transparent PNG keeps the subject on its own with no background, ready to place in a design, presentation or website. Choose it when you will combine the image with something else later. When you pick white, colour, blur or image backgrounds, the result is flattened and saved as JPG, which is smaller and accepted by every marketplace and form. To make the PNG smaller afterwards, use [Compress Image](/compress-image/), which keeps transparency.

The background is scaled to cover the whole frame and centred, then your subject is placed on top with the same edge blending as the transparent version. For product photos, a subtle gradient or texture often looks more premium than pure white; for profile photos, a softly blurred office or outdoor scene looks natural.

The model is designed for a single clear subject; it is not meant for removing small objects from a scene – use [Blur Face](/blur-face/) or an editor for that. What is WebP?

WebP is an image format developed by Google and released in 2010. It supports both lossy compression (like JPG) and lossless compression (like PNG), plus transparency and animation (like GIF) – all in one format. At the same visual quality, lossy WebP files are typically 25–35% smaller than JPG, and lossless WebP files are around 25% smaller than PNG. That is why websites, online shops and content delivery networks serve images as WebP whenever the browser supports it, and every major browser has supported it since 2020.

The downside is software outside the browser. Older versions of Windows Photo Viewer, Microsoft Office, Photoshop before version 23.2, many print services and plenty of upload forms do not accept WebP. Converting to JPG is the universal fix.

If a file is only going to be viewed in a browser or posted back to the web, there is no need to convert – WebP is smaller and every modern browser and most social networks accept it. Everything happens in your browser. The OCR engine and language models are loaded into the page and run on your device, so your images – ID cards, bank letters, medical reports, private messages – are never uploaded. There is no daily limit, no 'premium' accuracy tier and no account.

How OCR works

OCR turns pixels into characters in several stages. First the image is converted to black and white with adaptive thresholding, which copes with uneven lighting and coloured backgrounds. Then the page layout is analysed: the engine finds blocks of text, separates columns, and splits blocks into lines and words. Finally each line is fed to a neural network – an LSTM model trained on hundreds of thousands of lines of text in the chosen language – which predicts the most likely sequence of characters, using its knowledge of the language to choose between look-alikes like 'rn' and 'm' or '0' and 'O'.

{brand} uses Tesseract, the open-source OCR engine originally developed at HP and later maintained with Google's support, compiled to WebAssembly so it runs in the browser at near-native speed. The same engine powers many desktop and server OCR products.
Getting the most accurate results
**Use a sharp, well-lit image.** Blur and shadows are the main causes of errors. Photograph documents flat, in daylight, without the flash glare.
**Fill the frame with the text.** Crop away tables, hands and backgrounds with [Crop Image](/crop-image/).
**Choose the right language.** A French text read with the English model loses accents and misreads words.
**Increase DPI for small print.** If the text is small in the image, raise the resolution setting so letters are at least 20–30 pixels tall.
**Straighten the image.** Slight tilts are handled, but strongly rotated photos should be rotated first with [Rotate Image](/rotate-image/).
**Higher contrast helps.** Dark text on a light background gives the best results; light text on dark backgrounds usually works too.

Languages and scripts

Each language has its own trained model, which knows the alphabet and common words. Latin-script languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Italian) share most letters but differ in accents and vocabulary, so choosing the right one improves accuracy noticeably. Russian uses Cyrillic. Arabic is written right to left with letters that change shape depending on their position; the Arabic model handles this and outputs text in the correct logical order. Hindi uses Devanagari with its characteristic headline and conjunct letters, and Tamil has its own script with vowel signs around consonants – both have dedicated models. Chinese (Simplified) and Japanese have thousands of characters and larger models, so their first load takes a little longer.
For documents mixing two languages, choose both: every word is then matched against both models, which avoids, for example, English words being mangled in a Hindi document.
Text or searchable PDF?

Plain text is the most flexible: paste it into a document, e-mail, spreadsheet or translator. A searchable PDF keeps the image exactly as it looks and places the recognised text invisibly on top, so you can search it with Ctrl+F, select and copy passages, and let document management systems index it. Screenshots: the easiest case

Screenshots are ideal for OCR because the text is perfectly sharp, straight and evenly lit. To grab text from a video, a locked PDF, an app that does not allow copying, or an image in a chat, take a screenshot (Windows: Win+Shift+S; Mac: Cmd+Shift+4; Android and iPhone: the usual button combination), then open this page and press Ctrl+V. Extracting text from social media and memes

Images shared on social networks are usually compressed and may have text over busy backgrounds or coloured gradients. OCR still works well on large captions and on screenshots of posts, tweets and comments. For meme-style white text with black outlines, the engine reads the letters as long as they are big and clear; crop away the picture underneath to reduce noise. Very small text in compressed images – such as a watermark or a username in the corner – may need a higher DPI setting or a cleaner source image. If a post is still online, taking a fresh full-resolution screenshot gives better results than re-saving an already compressed copy several times.
Photos taken with a phone

Phone photos of documents vary much more than scans. For best results hold the phone parallel to the page so the text is not distorted in perspective, make sure the whole page is in focus by tapping on the text before shooting, and avoid your own shadow by standing to the side of the light source. Turn off the flash for glossy paper, which reflects light and creates white patches with no text. If you shoot in HEIC on an iPhone, you can upload the HEIC directly; it is decoded in the browser. A modern phone camera produces 12 megapixels or more, which is plenty – there is no need to raise the DPI setting for photos.
Receipts and invoices

Receipts are often printed on thermal paper, which fades over time and has low contrast. Photograph them soon after purchase, on a dark background so the edges are clear, and flatten curled paper. The OCR output will give you the shop name, items and totals as text you can paste into an expense spreadsheet. Because amounts are critical, check the totals by eye before submitting a claim.
OCR versus copying text from a PDF

If a PDF was created from a word processor, it already contains real text, and you can simply select and copy it or use [PDF to Text](/pdf-to-text/) – faster and 100% accurate. OCR is only needed when the PDF is a scan or a picture of text. A quick test: try to select a word in your PDF viewer. Glossary
**OCR (optical character recognition):** converting images of text into machine-readable characters.
**DPI (dots per inch):** how many pixels are used per inch of the original; higher values make small letters larger for the engine.
**Text layer:** invisible text placed over an image in a PDF so it can be searched and copied.
**LSTM:** the type of neural network used by modern Tesseract to recognise whole lines of text.
**Binarisation:** converting the image to pure black and white before recognition.

Nothing is uploaded, nothing is stored on a server and there is no queue, so private photos, ID cards, screenshots with personal data and unreleased product shots never leave your computer or phone. You can even switch off Wi‑Fi once the page has loaded and the tool keeps working.

Many online OCR services upload your image to a server and process it there, and some keep a history of conversions in an account. Here, the only thing downloaded is the language model – from our own site – and the only thing produced is text on your screen.

sections: Make small images bigger – without the blocky look

When you stretch a small image in a basic editor, it turns blocky or blurry: each original pixel simply becomes a square of identical pixels, or edges are smeared out. {brand}'s Upscale Image tool enlarges photos, graphics and screenshots by 1.5×, 2×, 3×, 4× or 8× using high-quality Lanczos resampling, optional denoising that cleans up JPEG artefacts before enlarging, and an unsharp mask that restores crispness afterwards. Some online upscalers use large generative AI models on their servers that 'invent' plausible new detail – skin pores, hair strands, brick texture. {brand} does not do that. It uses a mathematically precise resampling filter (Lanczos-3, the same family of filters used in professional image editors) plus classic cleanup and sharpening. This means it never adds details that were not there, never changes faces or text, and never produces the strange artefacts AI models sometimes create – but it also cannot reconstruct detail that the small image does not contain. For most uses – printing a web image larger, preparing a logo for a slide, enlarging a product photo for a marketplace, making a screenshot readable – careful resampling is exactly what you need, and it is fast and fully private.
Features
**Scale factors:** 1.5×, 2×, 3×, 4× and 8×.
**Lanczos-3 resampling** implemented separately for width and height for smooth, ringing-controlled edges.
**Denoise / JPEG cleanup:** off, light or strong, applied before enlarging so blocks and noise are not magnified.

How to upscale an image
Drop one or more images onto the page (or paste with Ctrl+V).
Choose the scale: 2× for most uses, 4× or 8× for very small sources.
For JPGs from the web or messaging apps, set Denoise to Light.
Leave Sharpen at Medium, or choose Strong for text and line art.
Click Upscale and compare with the slider, then download.
Which scale should I choose?

Remember that the visual quality of the result is limited by the information in the original. Going from 500 to 1000 pixels usually looks excellent; going from 100 to 800 pixels gives a smooth but soft image.
How Lanczos resampling works

Every pixel in the enlarged image lies between pixels of the original. The simplest method, nearest-neighbour, copies the closest original pixel – fast but blocky. Bilinear interpolation averages the four nearest pixels – smooth but blurry. Bicubic uses sixteen pixels and gives better results. Lanczos goes further: for each new pixel it looks at six original pixels in each direction and weights them by a windowed sinc function, the mathematically ideal reconstruction filter for band-limited signals. In practice this preserves edges and fine textures much better than bilinear or bicubic, while keeping halos small.

Because large upscales with one big step can amplify problems, {brand} applies the filter separately horizontally and vertically, which is both faster and exact for this kind of filter. The optional unsharp mask then increases local contrast at edges, which our eyes perceive as sharpness.
Denoise before you upscale

Images saved as JPG – especially those downloaded from social networks or forwarded through messaging apps – contain compression artefacts: faint 8×8 pixel blocks, ringing around text and colour smudges. Upscaling makes these four or sixteen times bigger and much more visible. The Denoise option applies a gentle blur before enlarging, which smooths the artefacts away; the sharpening step afterwards then restores edges. Use Light for normal web images and Strong for very compressed ones. For clean PNG graphics and photos straight from a camera, leave denoise off.
Use cases
**Printing:** web images are usually 72–150 pixels per inch at print size; upscaling 2–4× gets you closer to the 300 PPI printers like.
**E-commerce:** marketplaces often require a minimum of 1000–2000 pixels on the long side for zoom.
**Presentations:** enlarge logos and charts so they are not blurry on a projector.
**Old photos:** upscale scans of small prints before cropping or restoring.
**Games and pixel art:** 8× with sharpening off for crisp enlargements.
**Wallpapers:** take a favourite photo to Full HD or 4K.
**Social media:** meet the minimum resolution for cover and banner images.
Upscaling for print

Print quality depends on pixels per inch at the final size. A 1200×800 photo printed 10 cm wide has about 300 pixels per inch – excellent. The same photo printed 30 cm wide has only 100 – visibly soft up close. Upscaling 3× before printing does not add real detail, but it gives the printer a smooth image instead of letting it enlarge with its own, usually simpler, interpolation; edges and gradients look cleaner. For posters viewed from a distance, 150 PPI is often enough. After upscaling, use [Resize Image](/resize-image/) with centimetre or inch units to set the exact print size and DPI.
Tips for the best results
Start from the largest, least compressed version of the image you have.
Crop first, so you only enlarge what you need – [Crop Image](/crop-image/).
Use PNG output for graphics and screenshots, JPG at high quality for photos.
For text and logos, choose Strong sharpening; for faces, Medium looks more natural.
Avoid upscaling the same image repeatedly; one larger step is better than several small ones.
If the file becomes too big, compress it afterwards with [Compress Image](/compress-image/).

sections: Lanczos is often chosen as the reference method in image-processing libraries because it gives the best balance between sharpness and artefacts among classical filters. Combined with light sharpening, the difference from AI upscaling is small for moderate factors such as 2×, and Lanczos has the advantage of being completely predictable.
Upscaling different kinds of images

**Portraits and faces.** Use 2× or 3×, Denoise Light and Sharpen Medium. Strong sharpening on skin exaggerates pores and noise. Because nothing is invented, the person looks exactly like themselves – a common complaint about AI upscalers is that they subtly change facial features.

**Text, documents and screenshots.** Use 2×, Denoise Off and Sharpen Strong, and save as PNG. Letters become smooth and readable, ideal before printing or pasting into a report. If you want to copy the text, use [Image to Text](/image-to-text/) – upscaling small screenshots first can also improve OCR accuracy.

**Logos and icons.** Use 4×, Sharpen Strong, PNG output so transparency is kept. For truly scalable logos, a vector (SVG) version is always better than any upscale; ask the designer or brand owner for it.
**Product photos.** Use 2–3× with Light denoise and Medium sharpening. Combine with [Remove Background](/remove-background/) for a clean white background required by many marketplaces.
**Anime, cartoons and illustrations.** Flat colours and clean lines upscale very well with Lanczos. Use Strong sharpening and PNG.

**Old scanned photos.** Scan at the highest resolution your scanner supports first – that captures far more real detail than any upscaler. Then use Light or Strong denoise to reduce grain before enlarging.
How upscaling affects file size

Doubling width and height multiplies the number of pixels by four; 4× multiplies it by sixteen and 8× by sixty-four. A 1 MB JPG upscaled 4× can become 8–15 MB, and as a PNG it may exceed 50 MB. If you need a smaller file, choose JPG or WebP output, or run the result through [Compress Image](/compress-image/) with a target size. For web use, upscaling beyond the size at which the image is displayed only makes pages slower – resize to the display size instead.
Pixels, DPI and PPI explained

An image file only has pixels – for example 2400×1600. DPI or PPI (dots or pixels per inch) is a separate number that tells printers how large to print it. Changing DPI from 72 to 300 without changing pixels does not improve quality; it only makes the print smaller. To print larger at the same quality, you need more pixels, which is what upscaling gives you. A useful rule: pixels needed = print size in inches × 300 for close viewing, × 150 for posters. An A4 page (8.3×11.7 in) at 300 PPI needs about 2480×3508 pixels.

sections: When an AI upscaler might be better

If your image is extremely small (for example a 150-pixel thumbnail) and you need to print it large, or it is badly blurred, a generative AI service may produce a more impressive-looking result by hallucinating texture. Keep in mind that such services usually require uploading the image, often limit free use with credits or watermarks, and the added detail is not real – so they are unsuitable for evidence, documents, scientific images or anything where accuracy matters. For everyday enlargement, private on-device resampling is usually the safer and faster choice.
Upscaling on phones and tablets

The tool works in mobile Chrome, Safari and Firefox. Choose a photo from your gallery or take one with the camera. Phones have less memory than computers, so for large photos stay with 2× or 3×; 8× of a 12-megapixel photo would be far beyond the 64-megapixel limit anyway. On iPhone, HEIC photos are accepted directly. Downloads are saved to your Files or Downloads folder, from where you can share them or save them to your photo library.
Recommended minimum sizes for popular uses

Platforms change their recommendations from time to time, so check the current guidance before a big campaign. If your image is below the minimum, upscale it to just above the target, then use [Resize Image](/resize-image/) presets to hit the exact dimensions.
Using the before/after slider

After processing, drag the divider across the preview to compare the original (enlarged with simple browser scaling) and the {brand} result at the same size. Look at edges, text and areas of fine texture such as hair or fabric. If you see halos – light or dark outlines around edges – reduce sharpening. If flat areas look grainy, increase denoise. Because processing is local and fast, you can try two or three combinations in under a minute and keep the one you like best.
Common myths about upscaling
**'Upscaling recovers the original detail.'** Only the original camera or file has that detail; resampling reconstructs smooth transitions, and AI guesses texture.
**'Changing DPI to 300 makes it high resolution.'** DPI is only print metadata – pixels are what count.
**'Bigger is always better.'** An image larger than where it will be shown wastes storage and bandwidth.
**'You need a powerful server.'** Modern browsers compute even 64-megapixel results on an ordinary laptop in seconds.
Batch upscaling workflow

To prepare a whole product catalogue or photo album, drop all images at once. Each is enlarged with the same settings and named after the original with a suffix, so you can match them easily; the set is downloaded as one ZIP. Process images of similar type together – photos in one batch, logos and screenshots in another – because they benefit from different denoise and sharpening settings.
Upscaling and transparency

PNG and WebP images with transparent backgrounds – logos, stickers, cut-out product shots – keep their transparency when upscaled, as long as you choose PNG or WebP output. The resampling filter processes the alpha channel together with colour, so edges stay smooth instead of developing a jagged or coloured fringe. Choosing JPG output fills transparent areas with white, which is useful when a marketplace requires a white background but not when you want to place the image over other content. If your cut-out comes from [Remove Background](/remove-background/), upscale it as PNG and then place it on any background you like. For best results with very fine edges like hair, upscale first and then remove the background, so the cut-out works on more pixels.
Glossary
**Upscaling:** increasing an image's pixel dimensions.
**Resampling:** computing new pixel values from the original ones when changing size.
**Lanczos filter:** a high-quality resampling filter based on the sinc function.
**Unsharp mask:** a sharpening technique that boosts the difference between the image and a blurred copy.
**Artefacts:** unwanted patterns such as JPEG blocks, halos or noise.
**Megapixel:** one million pixels; 8000×8000 is 64 megapixels.
Privacy

Every step happens inside your browser tab. The image is decoded, edited and re-encoded on your own device using the browser's built-in image engine and WebAssembly, and the result is handed straight to your downloads folder. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is stored on a server and there is no queue, so private photos, ID cards, screenshots with personal data and unreleased product shots never leave your computer or phone. You can even switch off Wi‑Fi once the page has loaded and the tool keeps working.
Many AI upscalers upload your image to their servers and keep it for a period – often up to 24 hours – before deleting it. Here, there is nothing to delete: the image never leaves your device.

Static vs dynamic QR codes

There are two kinds of QR codes on the market. A **static** code encodes your content directly – the URL, the Wi-Fi details – in the black and white pattern. A **dynamic** code encodes a short link to the provider's server, which then redirects to your real URL. Dynamic codes let you change the destination later and count scans, but they only work while you keep paying the provider: if the subscription lapses, or the provider closes, every printed code stops working. sections: Designing a QR code that always scans
**Keep strong contrast.** Dark modules on a light background. Light-on-dark (inverted) codes are not read by some older scanners.
**Don't over-style.** Dots and gradients look great; check that the darkest and lightest colours still differ clearly.
**Keep the quiet zone.** The white margin around the code (at least four modules) helps cameras find it – don't crop it away.
**Logos up to about 20–25% of the area.** Larger logos hide too many modules even at level H.
**Shorter content = bigger modules.** A short URL produces a simpler code that scans from further away.
**Always test** with two or three phones – iPhone camera, Android camera and a scanner app – before printing thousands of copies.
Error correction levels

QR codes contain redundant data so they still work when part of the code is damaged, dirty or covered by a logo. There are four levels: L recovers about 7% of damaged data, M about 15%, Q about 25% and H about 30%. Higher levels make the code denser. Use M for clean digital use, Q for outdoor print, and H when you add a logo – {brand} switches to H automatically when you upload one.
Print size and scanning distance

A useful rule of thumb is that a QR code can be scanned from about ten times its width: a 2 cm code from 20 cm, a 10 cm code on a poster from about 1 metre, and a 1 m code on a banner from about 10 metres. For business cards, 2–2.5 cm is the practical minimum. For printing, use SVG or PDF so the edges stay perfectly sharp at any size, or PNG at 2000 pixels or more.
Wi-Fi QR codes

A Wi-Fi code lets guests join your network by pointing their camera at it – no spelling out long passwords. Enter the network name (SSID) exactly as it appears, the password, and the security type (WPA/WPA2/WPA3 for almost all modern routers, WEP for very old ones, or none for open networks). Tick 'hidden' if your network does not broadcast its name. iPhones (iOS 11 and later) and Android phones (10 and later) support Wi-Fi codes from the built-in camera. For a dedicated page with tips, see [Wi-Fi QR Code Generator](/wifi-qr-code-generator/).
vCard QR codes for business cards

A vCard code holds your name, company, job title, phones, e-mail, website and address. When scanned, the phone offers to save the contact – no typing, no misspelled e-mail addresses. Keep it compact: every extra field adds data and makes the code denser, so on a small business card include only what people really need. See [vCard QR Code Generator](/vcard-qr-code-generator/) for a dedicated form.
Privacy

The QR code is generated entirely in your browser. What you type – web addresses, Wi-Fi passwords, phone numbers, contact details – is never sent to {brand} or anyone else. The resulting static code does not redirect through any server, so no one tracks who scans it, when or where.
Dynamic-code providers, by contrast, sit between every person who scans your code and your website and record scan data. That can be useful for marketing, but it is worth knowing before you print.
How a QR code works

QR stands for 'Quick Response'. The format was invented in 1994 by Denso Wave, a Toyota group company, to track car parts, and is now an international standard (ISO/IEC 18004). A QR code is a grid of square modules. The three large squares in the corners – the finder patterns or 'eyes' – let the camera locate the code and work out its angle. Smaller alignment patterns correct for perspective, timing lines set the grid, and format information tells the reader which error-correction level and mask are used. The rest of the grid holds your data, encoded with Reed–Solomon error correction, the same mathematics that lets scratched CDs play.

Codes come in 40 versions, from 21×21 modules (version 1) to 177×177 (version 40). The more data you encode and the higher the error correction, the larger the version – which is why a long URL with a logo produces a denser code than a short link without one. A version 40 code can hold up to about 4,296 alphanumeric characters, but for reliable scanning on phones, staying well below a few hundred characters is wise.

sections: A simple test: convert your design to greyscale in your head – if the modules and background would be clearly different shades of grey, it will scan. Printing can also shift colours, particularly on uncoated or coloured paper, so print a test copy first.
PNG, SVG or PDF?

**PNG** is a pixel image, perfect for websites, slides, social posts and e-mail. Choose a size large enough for the use – 1000 pixels for screens, 2000–4000 for print. **SVG** is a vector format: the code is stored as shapes, so it can be enlarged to any size, from a sticker to a building wrap, without blur. Designers can open it in Illustrator, Inkscape, Figma or Affinity and change colours. **PDF** is ready to send to a printer or to place in a document; when you use gradients, frames or a logo, the PDF contains a high-resolution image of your styled code.
QR codes for restaurants and cafés

Menu codes on tables are one of the most popular uses. Link to a menu page on your own website, or to a PDF menu hosted on your site, rather than to a third-party dynamic link that may expire. Print codes 4–5 cm wide on table tents, add a frame with the text 'Scan for menu', and laminate them against spills. Put a Wi-Fi code next to it so guests can join your network instantly. If you update the menu, update the page or replace the PDF at the same address – the printed codes keep working.
Packaging, products and labels

On product packaging, QR codes link to instructions, ingredient lists, warranty registration, videos or reorder pages. Use a short URL so the code stays small and simple, keep it away from folds and curved edges, and use SVG so the printer gets perfectly sharp edges. On small labels, choose error correction M without a logo to keep modules as large as possible.
Events, flyers and posters

Event codes can add the date, time and place directly to a phone's calendar. Location codes open the venue in the map app. On posters, put the code at chest height, add a clear call to action ('Scan for tickets') in the frame, and make sure there is enough light where the poster hangs. Codes behind glass work, but avoid reflective lamination that creates glare.
Safety: QR code scams

Because people cannot read a QR code by eye, criminals sometimes stick fake codes over real ones on parking meters, posters or restaurant tables to send people to phishing pages – a scam sometimes called 'quishing'. If you place codes in public, check them regularly, consider tamper-evident stickers, and print your domain name under the code so people can see where it leads. When you scan a code yourself, check the URL preview your phone shows before opening it, and never enter passwords or payment details on a page reached from an unexpected code. You can check any code's contents safely with our [QR Code Scanner](/qr-code-scanner/).
Pre-print checklist
Scan with at least two different phones from the intended distance.
Check that the link opens the right page on mobile – and that the page loads quickly.
Keep a quiet zone of at least four modules on every side.
Use SVG or PDF for professional printing.
Print a test copy on the final paper and test in the final lighting.
Add a short call to action so people know why they should scan.
Keep a copy of the content (URL, Wi-Fi password) in case you need to recreate the code.
Glossary
**Module:** one square 'pixel' of the QR code grid.
**Finder pattern / eye:** the three large squares in the corners.
**Quiet zone:** the empty margin around the code.
**Error correction (L/M/Q/H):** redundancy that lets damaged codes still scan.
**Static code:** data stored directly in the code; never expires.
**Dynamic code:** a short redirect link managed by a provider; can be edited and tracked.
**Version:** the size of the grid, from 21×21 to 177×177 modules.
How to scan a QR code

On an **iPhone**, open the Camera app and point it at the code; a banner with the link appears – tap it. You can also add the Code Scanner to Control Centre. On **Android**, open the camera (most phones since Android 9 scan automatically) or use Google Lens from the search bar or camera app. On a **computer**, upload a screenshot or photo of the code to our [QR Code Scanner](/qr-code-scanner/). Wi-Fi, contact and event codes trigger the matching action – join network, save contact, add to calendar – instead of opening a link.
Using a logo well

A logo makes a code instantly recognisable and increases trust, but it covers part of the data. Use a simple, high-contrast version of your logo – an icon or monogram rather than a full wordmark – on a square or circular image, ideally with a white or transparent background. Keep it to roughly a fifth of the code's width. Since the code relies on error correction to work around the logo, avoid combining a large logo with very long content, which makes modules small and leaves less margin for error. If you only have a logo with a busy background, cut it out first with [Remove Background](/remove-background/).
Frames and calls to action

A bare QR code tells people nothing about what they will get; a short instruction next to it gives them a reason to pick up their phone. Use the frame option to add a label such as 'Scan for menu', 'Scan to join Wi-Fi', 'Scan for 10% off' or 'Watch the video'. The 'label below' frame adds a text strip under the code; 'box with label' surrounds the code with a coloured border, which also guarantees a clean quiet zone when the code is placed on busy backgrounds or photographs. Keep the label to two to four words so it stays readable at small sizes.
Accessibility

Not everyone can scan a code – some people have older phones, visual impairments or simply prefer not to. Whenever space allows, print a short, readable URL or phone number next to the code as an alternative, and use descriptive alt text when you place a QR image on a website. On screens, a QR code is mainly useful for moving from a desktop to a phone; on the phone itself, a normal link is always easier than a code.
QR codes in documents and presentations

Adding a QR code to a slide lets the audience open your resources, survey or contact page while you are still speaking. Place it in a corner of the final slide, at least a fifth of the slide height, and leave it on screen long enough for people at the back to scan. In reports, CVs and printed handouts, a small code beside a link saves readers from typing long addresses. Download PNG at 1000 pixels for PowerPoint, Google Slides or Keynote, or SVG for Word and InDesign layouts where it must stay crisp. You can also put a code into an existing PDF – such as a flyer or ticket – with [Add Image to PDF](/add-image-to-pdf/). For multi-page documents, consider a different code on each section page so readers jump straight to the relevant online material instead of a general homepage.
